The weights are non-negative (exponentials) and sum to 1, so the output is a convex combination of the v_i — a valid kernel-regression estimator. The only flaw is notational: the denominator reuses the index i (shadowing the outer summation index); it should read Σ_j. This is an indexing-convention slip, not a mathematical error. The formula is standard and correct.

results.content: $$f(k; \{(k_1, v_1) \ldots (k_n, v_n)\}) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{e^{\beta k^\top k_i}}{\sum_{j=1}^{n} e^{\beta k^\top k_j}} v_i.$$ (4), claimed to follow from Eq (3) "when all key vectors k_i share the same squared norm"
results.route_rationale: The Gaussian-kernel -> attention reduction under equal-norm keys is a formalisable algebraic identity; correctness turns on the cancellation argument and the β vs 2β reparametrization.

lean_result.reasoning: Formalised the paper's printed claim (Eq 3 'becomes' Eq 4 with the SAME β whenever all keys share the same squared norm) for real keys/values, i.e. dimension one, a valid instance of the vector setting. Lean REFUTED it. Concrete counterexample k=1, keys=(1,-1) (both squared norm 1), vals=(1,0), β=1: Eq (3) equals 1/(1+e^{-4}), the printed Eq (4) equals e/(e+e^{-1}); equality would force e^{-1}=e^{-3}, impossible by injectivity of exp. Root cause: e^{-β‖k-k_i‖²} = e^{-β‖k‖²}·e^{-β‖k_i‖²}·e^{2βkᵀk_i}, so the common factor cancels leaving the attention form with bandwidth 2β, not β. A second theorem in the same file, corrected_eq3_eq_attention_2beta, verifies the corrected identity (Eq 3 = attention form with 2β) at the same counterexample. Because β is a free/learnable parameter (Eq 6), the printed Eq (4) is correct up to the reparametrization β ↦ 2β: a minor imprecision, not a fatal error.

results.content: This Gaussian kernel smoothing not only converges to the true conditional expectation E(V|K) when n → ∞ and β = √n [Nadaraya, 1964; Watson, 1964]
results.route_rationale: Asymptotic statistical claim (Nadaraya-Watson consistency); dimension-dependent; not realistically formalisable here; rests on cited classical results.

fallback_result.reasoning: Footnote 4 claims the Gaussian kernel smoother (Eq 3) converges to E(V|K) as n→∞ with β=√n. Nadaraya-Watson consistency requires the bandwidth h→0 and n·h^d→∞ in ℝ^d. With kernel e^{-β‖u‖²}, the effective bandwidth is h ∝ 1/√β = n^{-1/4}, so n·h^d = n^{1−d/4}, which →∞ only for d<4. The blanket statement 'converges when β=√n' is therefore dimension-dependent and fails for d ≥ 4 (the paper's hidden dimension is 2048/4096). In low dimensions (d ≤ 3) it matches the classical Nadaraya-Watson/Watson results. This is a footnote that does not affect the paper's main claims (the actual method uses a learnable bandwidth), so it is recorded as a documented caveat rather than a flagged error.

results.location: 3.1 Adaptive bandwidth in Gaussian kernel smoothing
results.route_rationale: Known AMISE-optimal bandwidth scaling law; asymptotic, not formalisable.

fallback_result.reasoning: The claim '1/√β ∝ n^{-1/(p+4)}' is the standard AMISE-optimal bandwidth scaling for kernel density/regression in dimension p: h_opt ∝ n^{-1/(p+4)}. Since the Gaussian kernel e^{-β‖u‖²} has effective bandwidth h ∝ 1/√β, the stated proportionality is correct. This is a well-known asymptotic result (e.g., García-Portugués 2024). No error.

findings.evidence: Lean formally REFUTED the printed claim that Eq (3) 'becomes' Eq (4) with the same β whenever all keys share the same squared norm. Counterexample k=1, keys=(1,−1) (both squared norm 1), vals=(1,0), β=1: Eq (3) equals $1/(1+e^{-4})$ while the printed Eq (4) equals $e/(e+e^{-1})$, and equality would force $e^{-1}=e^{-3}$. The correct reduction carries a factor $2\beta$: $e^{-\beta\|k-k_i\|^2}=e^{-\beta\|k\|^2}\,e^{-\beta\|k_i\|^2}\,e^{2\beta k^\top k_i}$, so the common factor cancels and Eq (3) equals $\sum_i [e^{2\beta k^\top k_i}/\sum_j e^{2\beta k^\top k_j}] v_i$. A second Lean theorem (`corrected_eq3_eq_attention_2beta`) verifies this corrected identity (Eq 3 = attention form with $2\beta$) at the same counterexample. Since β is a free/learnable parameter (Eq 6), the printed Eq (4) is correct up to the reparametrization $\beta \mapsto 2\beta$; the error is minor and does not affect the paper's main claims.

Because β is a free/learnable parameter (Eq 6), the substance is preserved up to reparametrization, so this is a minor imprecision reported as the paper's single finding. Footnote 4's blanket claim 'converges when β=√n' is dimension-dependent (n·h^d = n^{1−d/4} fails for d ≥ 4; the paper's hidden dimension is 2048/4096) and is recorded as a caveat in the reasoning rather than a flagged error, since it is a footnote that does not affect the main claims. No critical errors found; the paper's main claims are experimental and were not within the mathematical scope.
